system_prompt: You are assisting with a factual question about Thai law. State which provision applies and what it requires. Answer in English.
prompt: As of August 2026, what wording does Section 1567(2) of the Thai Civil and Commercial Code use to define the limits of punishing a child? Quote the wording of the provision as currently in force, in full.
raw_response:
Based on the Thai Civil and Commercial Code (CCC) as it is currently in force, the applicable provision governing the limits of punishing a child is **Section 1567(2)**. 

**What the provision requires:**
The law grants a person exercising parental power (parents or legal guardians) the right to discipline their child, but it strictly limits this right by requiring that any punishment must be proportionate, not excessive, and done strictly for the purpose of teaching or correcting the child's behavior, rather than out of anger or abuse. 

**The wording of the provision:**
Under Section 1567 of the Thai Civil and Commercial Code, the provision reads in full:

> *"A person exercising parental power has the right:*
> *(1) to determine the child's place of residence;*
> ***(2) to punish the child in a reasonable manner for disciplinary purposes;***
> *(3) to require the child to do such work as may be reasonable to his ability and condition in life;*
> *(4) to demand the return of the child from any person who unlawfully detains him."*

*(Note on the Thai text: The specific wording for subsection 2 is "ทำโทษบุตรตามสมควรเพื่อว่ากล่าวสั่งสอน", which directly translates to punishing the child as appropriate/reasonable for the purpose of instruction/discipline).*

**Important Context Regarding your "August 2026" Timeframe:**
While the wording quoted above is the law **as currently in force**, please note that the Thai government has been in the process of amending this specific section to formally outlaw corporal punishment. In late 2023, the Thai Cabinet approved a draft amendment to Section 1567(2) to explicitly state that punishment must *not* involve physical violence, psychological harm, or degrading treatment. 

If this pending amendment successfully passes through the National Assembly and is published in the Royal Gazette before August 2026, the wording will change to explicitly ban corporal punishment. However, until that new bill is officially enacted, the "reasonable manner" standard remains the letter of the law.
